Data description

We conduct this study using data from Sweden for a number of reasons. First, virtually
all businesses are required by law to file audited financial statements. <sup>14</sup> Second, Sweden
has long required the audit partner to sign the opinion. Third, we are able to identify
many attributes of individual partners from regulatory filings. These conditions enable us
to construct virtually the entire client portfolio for a large sample of individual auditors in
Big 4 firms. This allows us to examine the pattern of audit judgment for an individual
audit partner across all of their clients and across time. Information on the identity of
individual auditors is obtained from Finansinspektionen (Swedish Financial Supervisory
Authority). The data include all auditors who acted as a lead or deputy auditor for at

13. Cassar (2011) notes that research on private company lending suggests that third-party credit scores provide an alternative channel for reducing information asymmetries by offering lenders a cost-effective and
timely means of monitoring borrowers (See also Petersen and Rajan 2002; Berger and Frame 2007).
14. During our data period from 2001 to 2008, all public and private Swedish companies regardless of their
size were required to be audited. In 2008, there were around 330,000 audits of limited liability companies
conducted by a total of 4,108 individual auditors (SOU 2008, 32:134). Effective in November 1, 2010, statutory audits are required for companies meeting at least two of the following criteria: (i) average number
of employees more than three, (ii) total assets of more than 1.5 million SEK, and (iii) sales of more than
3 million SEK. Company accounts must be filed annually within seven months of the year-end and are
available to the public when filed.

dates that partners received their certifications come from the Revisorsnamnden€ (The

information about bankruptcy filings, credit ratings, and risk forecasts are obtained from
UC AB, a leading business and credit information agency in Sweden.

For this study, we require an auditor to appear in the sample for a minimum of
four consecutive years. We use at least two years as an estimation period to calculate
prior error frequencies. We use subsequent years for our empirical tests (i.e., in year
2008, error frequencies are based on the prior seven years if an auditor appears in the
data each year). This is suggested by Beyer and Sridhar 2006 and assumes that the
quality of an auditor is revealed over time. We exclude clients of non-Big 4 auditors
and clients employing joint audits to avoid confounding firm and auditor choice effects
(Teoh and Wong 1993). We exclude finance and insurance industries due to their
unique accounting and regulations (Butler, Leone, and Willenborg 2004; Carey and Simnett 2006). We also delete firm-years with negative total assets and observations with
leverage ratios less than zero (Cai and Zhang 2011). <sup>15</sup> The number of observations varies across the different tests due to the use of different subsamples and limitations arising from the calculations of the dependent and explanatory variables. Table 1
